source_defaults.notes: Original candidate-controlled congressional campaign pages retained in actual pre-primary archive versions. The June2017 Westbrook pages precede the special-election announcement but explicitly identify the same2018 Arizona8 congressional candidacy; they are early campaign positions, not proof every detail remained unchanged until February27. Article bylines, template edit timestamps and copyright years are not promoted to first-publication dates. Candidate factual, medical, legal and fiscal claims remain attributed, not independently verified. Later state-house material reached through redirects is excluded from this congressional comparison.

sources.speaker: Brianna Westbrook
sources.notes: Original June12,2017 congressional issue page. Repeated reproductive-rights, gun and climate paragraphs are preserved in the complete download but enrolled only once. The repeated sections do not create independent evidence.

sources.speaker: Brianna Westbrook
sources.notes: Original candidate-authored single-payer article, actual December16,2017 replay. Paragraph22 says expansion of Medicaid while the heading in paragraph25 says Medicare for All. Preserve the program-name inconsistency. The unambiguous commitments are tax-financed single payer, private delivery, removal of financial barriers and elimination of private health insurers; do not silently change Medicaid to Medicare.

sources.speaker: Hiral Tipirneni
sources.notes: The page is an official Hiral campaign platform, not a claim that Hiral personally typed each word. It has a staff/template author label, and explicitly describes District8 economic proposals. The existing retained copy includes archive chrome; this exact replay is separately retained and the same substantive text is deduplicated downstream.

statements.claim: Explicitly supports tax-financed single payer delivered through private facilities. The text names Medicaid here but Medicare for All in a heading, so program terminology is flagged rather than silently corrected.
Explicitly proposes eliminating private health insurers, while separately retaining private medical delivery. Insurers and healthcare providers are not conflated.
Directly calls single payer the top priority of her Arizona8 congressional campaign. This is an explicit self-reported priority, not a frequency estimate.

Her earlier2017 issue page explicitly opposes ACA repeal and affirms access regardless of income or pre-existing conditions. This is compatible with her later single-payer proposal rather than proof of opposition to all existing ACA protections.
Supports tuition-free community college and state universities.
Proposes loan forgiveness for current teachers, not every student borrower.
Supports teacher pay commensurate with educational responsibilities.
Proposes incentives for businesses and households using renewables, plus research to lower clean-energy costs.
Commits to protecting women against job discrimination, alongside STEM grants and reproductive-rights proposals.
Supports paid parental leave for mothers and fathers with protection against losing their jobs.
Opposes benefit cuts and commits to preserving Social Security and Medicare for future beneficiaries.
Proposes legislation supporting access to addiction treatment and recovery resources. This is a policy commitment, not treatment advice.
Supports a woman's choice and opposes defunding Planned Parenthood. The duplicated source paragraph is not counted twice.
Supports stronger screening and background checks while affirming Second Amendment rights and cross-party compromise. Her description of purchase rules is not current legal guidance.

Frames education cuts and corporate tax preferences as exploitation of working and poor families, and asks voters to support pro-education candidates. These are attributed campaign arguments, not independently audited fiscal findings.
Supports retaining popular ACA protections on dependent coverage, pre-existing conditions, benefit caps and basic services, while repairing flaws.
Proposes competition between private insurance and Medicare as a route to cost containment and improved care. This retains private insurers, unlike Westbrook's explicit elimination proposal.

statements.quote: good ideas can come from anywhere
statements.claim: Frames healthcare reform through practical ideas from both political sides and a combined coverage/cost approach.
Proposes expanded workforce development and apprenticeships aligned with secondary and post-secondary education, plus retraining for emerging jobs.
Supports expanded access to affordable childcare.
Explicitly calls for equal pay for women doing the same work as men.
Proposes job protection during medical or family emergencies. This line does not specify paid leave, so payment is not inferred.
Supports simplifying taxes and closing loopholes so reform chiefly benefits the middle class.
Frames federal economic policy as expanding opportunity while preserving success, with workforce, healthcare and family-support proposals.

comparisons.analysis: Westbrook expressly proposes tax-financed single payer with private delivery. Tipirneni's previously reviewed plan allows people under65 to buy into Medicare while retaining private coverage. The Westbrook article's Medicaid/Medicare naming inconsistency remains explicit and does not erase the financing difference.

Westbrook explicitly proposes eliminating private health insurers. Tipirneni explicitly proposes competition between private insurers and Medicare. This is a directly supported disagreement about insurers, not a claim that either opposes private doctors or hospitals.

Both retain existing ACA coverage protections: Westbrook explicitly opposes repeal in her earlier issue page, and Tipirneni names protections to preserve. Their broader financing differences do not imply Westbrook supports stripping current coverage.

Westbrook specifies free public-college tuition; Tipirneni emphasizes workforce development, apprenticeships and alignment with education. These can coexist, and Tipirneni's unmentioned tuition policy is not coded as opposition.
Westbrook states a broad anti-discrimination commitment for women at work; Tipirneni specifies equal pay for equal work. The narrower proposition is not assumed to exhaust either platform.

Westbrook expressly proposes paid parental leave with job security. Tipirneni expressly proposes job security for family or medical emergencies but does not state paid status in this passage. The omission is not coded as rejecting paid leave.

Westbrook names single payer as her top congressional priority; Tipirneni foregrounds cross-party ideas combining coverage and cost control. These are the candidates' stated frames, not inferred from endorsement labels.

Westbrook presents education and tax conflicts through exploitation of poor and working families; Tipirneni presents an opportunity-and-innovation approach that should not penalize success. Both have specific education and family-support proposals; neither is reduced to a caricature.
